chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man comes to me seeking goods, so I negotiate with him on the profit, then I buy it and sell it to him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Is it not that if he desires, he takes it, and if he desires, he leaves it?' I said: 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem with it.'

I said: 'But one among us considers it invalid.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And why?' I said: 'Because he sells what is not with him.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'So what do you say regarding the sale of Salam (advance payment for goods), where its owner has sold what is not with him?' I said: 'Yes.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'It is valid only because they name it Salam. Indeed, my father used to say: There is no problem with selling every type of goods which you can find at the time in which you sell it.'

key_terms.السَّلَم: Salam, a specific type of forward sale contract in Islamic law where payment is made in advance for specified goods to be delivered later
key_terms.الْمَتَاع: Goods, merchandise, or items of trade
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no problem with it / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible in Shia jurisprudence to sell goods you do not yet own?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* clarifies the permissibility of *Bay' al-Ma'mul bihi* (selling what one intends to acquire) by distinguishing it from the formal *Salam* contract, noting that the Imam’s father, Imam al-Baqir, permitted selling any goods available at the time of fulfillment. It addresses the scholarly debate regarding the validity of such sales when the seller does not yet possess the item, affirming their permissibility based on the principle of actual availability at the time of delivery rather than immediate possession. This ruling supports commercial flexibility in Shia jurisprudence, allowing traders to negotiate profits on goods they are in the process of acquiring.
